purpose: Add eight source-exact Sir Robert Anderson excerpts for stewardship, grace, holiness, and Christian living.

defaults.author: Sir Robert Anderson
defaults.sourceTitle: The Way: Chapters on the Christian Life
defaults.rightsBasis: This 1905 James Nisbet edition is public domain; each excerpt is verified against the stored OCR and should be checked against the scan before publication.

entries.title: The present in view of the future
entries.text: The Christian acts in the present with a view to the future.
entries.slideText: The Christian acts in the present with a view to the future.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed transition into preaching about eternal priorities and present faithfulness.
entries.reviewNote: Avoid neglecting present responsibilities. Biblical hope orders faithful life now rather than encouraging escapism.

entries.title: God's servant in every sphere
entries.text: The Christian is as really God's servant in the one sphere as in the other.
entries.slideText: The Christian is as really God's servant in the one sphere as in the other.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed application against dividing life into sacred and secular compartments.
entries.reviewNote: Different callings carry different duties, but every lawful sphere belongs under Christ's lordship.

entries.title: Neither merit nor woe
entries.text: There is neither merit in being poor nor woe in being rich.
entries.slideText: There is neither merit in being poor nor woe in being rich.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed corrective before teaching biblical warnings and responsibilities concerning wealth and poverty.
entries.reviewNote: Do not minimize oppression or Scripture's warnings to the rich. Material condition neither earns salvation nor automatically proves condemnation.

entries.title: Salvation is God's gift
entries.text: Salvation is a gift — God's gift, bestowed on the principle of grace, received on the principle of faith.
entries.slideText: Salvation is a gift — God's gift
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed Gospel summary after reading and explaining the cited KJV passages.
entries.reviewNote: The quotation is a doctrinal summary, not Scripture. Explain repentance, faith, grace, and Christ's finished work directly from the KJV.

entries.title: Calvary surpasses words
entries.text: The Divine sacrifice of Calvary surpasses the power of words to tell it
entries.slideText: The Divine sacrifice of Calvary surpasses the power of words to tell it
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed reflective line after a Scripture-centered explanation of Christ's sacrifice.
entries.reviewNote: Keep the quotation subordinate to the KJV account of the cross and avoid relying on emotional language instead of doctrinal clarity.

entries.title: A positive and active principle
entries.text: a positive and active principle to mould and govern the Christian life.
entries.slideText: a positive and active principle to mould and govern the Christian life.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed phrase explaining that grace trains believers for godly living rather than excusing sin.
entries.reviewNote: The lowercase opening is an exact excerpt from a longer sentence. Display it with context or an ellipsis and visible attribution.

entries.title: The wonder of redemption
entries.text: The lasting wonder of redemption is that sinners can approach a holy God
entries.slideText: The lasting wonder of redemption is that sinners can approach a holy God
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed line of wonder before explaining the believer's access to God through Christ.
entries.reviewNote: The line is an incomplete excerpt and should be displayed with attribution. Explain access, cleansing, and holiness from the cited KJV texts.

entries.title: Boldness is not levity
entries.text: boldness is far removed from levity.
entries.slideText: boldness is far removed from levity.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed contrast when teaching both confident access to God and reverent worship.
entries.reviewNote: Biblical boldness is confidence through Christ, not casual irreverence. Let both cited KJV passages shape the application.
